newsitem.title: USA: Report finds flaws by FBI labs in major cases.
newsitem.headline: Report finds flaws by FBI labs in major cases.

text.p: The FBI's crime laboratories provided flawed evidence in some major cases, including the Oklahoma City and World Trade Center bombing cases, a Justice Department report said on Tuesday.
A report by the department's inspector general after an 18-month investigation recommended the removal of the heads of some laboratories and overhauling their operations.
But it questioned "the judgement and common sense" of Frederic Whitehurst, an agent who first alleged scientific fraud and slanting of evidence to favor prosecutors and was subsequently suspended.
"Most of Whitehurst's allegations were not substantiated," Inspector General Michael Bromwich wrote. "Some important ones were."

Bromwich, presenting his report at a news conference, added: "The problems and deficiencies that Whitehurst brought to our attention are extremely serious. But they are a far cry from the types of rampant and intentional wrongdoing alleged by Dr Whitehurst ... Although Whitehurst raised some valid concerns, we did not substantiate the majority of his allegations including his most inflammatory charges of perjury and fabrication of evidence."
Whitehiurst, interviewed by CNN said he was amazed at the conclusions critical of him.

Reading from the report, he said: "They had a felony finding of testimony beyond the examiner's expertise, improper preparation of laboratory reports, insufficient documentation of test results, scientifically flawed reports, inadequate record management, and it goes on and on and on. And yet at the end of this report I find that I have been accused of using poor judgment. That's amazing. That's amazing."

Addressing the flaws his investigation did turn up in FBI crime lab work, Bromwich said: "Our investigation found deficient work in some high-profile cases and also indentified policies and practices in need of substantial change."

He said examples of "serious and significant deficiencies" included "scientifically flawed testimony, inaccurate testimony, testimony beyond the laboratory examiner's expertise, improper preparation of laboratory reports, insufficient documentation of test results, scientifically flawed reports (and) inadequate record management ..."

In detailing mistakes and flawed testimony, the report is likely to help defense lawyers in major cases such as the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing. But Bromwich said that his findings "should in no circumstance be read as expressing a view as to whether that case should have reached a different outcome."
The report said that FBI officials involved in the Oklahoma City case "merit special censure" for evidence provided by explosives expert David Williams.
It accused him of basing his testimony about the size and type of the bomb that destroyed the building on materials a defendant had purchased, not on scientific grounds.
The report also found Williams gave inaccurate testimony on the bomb used in the 1993 World Trade Center case "that appeared to be tailored to the most incriminating result."

The two-volume report released by the Justice Department documented similar failings in such other high profile cases as the an Avianca Airlines jet in 1989 which exploded after taking off from Bogota.
The inspector general recommended that the heads of the FBI's explosives and chemical and toxic laboratories should be removed and Williams should be reassigned.
The inspector general, however, put almost as much emphasis on criticizing the "whistle-blower," Whitehurst, insisting his charges had been greatly exaggerated.

"Whitehurst alleged that many employees within the lab repeatedly committed perjury, fabricated evidence, obstructed justice and suppressed exculpatory evidence. Our careful and lengthy review failed to substantiate those charges," he said.

He said the "incendiary way" that Whitehurst, who was suspended pending the investigation, had criticized fellow laboratory workers would make it extremely difficult for him to work effectively in the institution in the future.
